```{r, load libraries}
#| output: FALSE
# Output false ensures your reproducible document does not show all of your code!

# Remember to install packages you do not already have

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(gt)
```

```{r, load data}
# The attitude dataset is built into R (datasets package), so no file import is needed.
# Keep only the outcome (rating) and the three predictors used in this lab.

attitude.data <- attitude |>
  select(rating, complaints, learning, raises)
```

```{r, descriptives}
descriptives <- attitude.data |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Value),
    SD   = sd(Value),
    Min  = min(Value),
    Max  = max(Value)
  )

descriptives |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Descriptive Statistics for Analysis Variables") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Mean, SD), decimals = 2)
```

```{r, rating histogram}
ggplot(attitude.data, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 10) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Overall Workplace Ratings",
       x = "Overall rating", y = "Density")
```

```{r, scatterplots}
ggplot(attitude.data, aes(x = complaints, y = rating)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Overall Rating by Complaint Handling",
       x = "Handling of complaints", y = "Overall rating")

ggplot(attitude.data, aes(x = learning, y = rating)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Overall Rating by Opportunity to Learn",
       x = "Opportunity to learn", y = "Overall rating")

ggplot(attitude.data, aes(x = raises, y = rating)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Overall Rating by Pay Increases",
       x = "Pay Increases", y = "Overall rating")
```

**1.4: Exploration of the Data**

All three predictors were positively associated with overall workplace ratings, and each relationship appeared approximately linear. Handling of employee complaints showed the strongest association, followed by opportunity to learn and performance-based raises based on the graphs. The raises relationship in particular showed more scatter around the fitted line. No departments appeared to be extreme outliers. With only 30 departments, individual observations may still carry influence, so this is examined further in the regression diagnostics.

These patterns are consistent with expectations: complaint handling reflects how responsive management is to employees, which is something employees are likely to expect regardless of their own performance. Learning opportunities and performance based raises on the other hand can depend on employees’ own effort, so they may shape overall impressions of the workplace less directly.

**2.1: Developing my Predictions**

I expected the handling of employee complaints to be the strongest predictor of overall workplace ratings, because it reflects how responsive management is to employees’ concerns, an aspect of the workplace that affects all employees regardless of their role or performance. I expected opportunities to learn to explain additional variation beyond complaint handling, since learning captures a distinct aspect of the workplace. However, because departments with responsive management may also tend to offer more learning opportunities, I expected part of the learning effect to overlap with complaint handling, so its unique contribution should be smaller than its association with ratings on its own. Finally, I expected performance-based raises to add relatively little once complaints and learning were accounted for, since they depend partly on employees’ own performance and they might not be strongly connected to quality of management.

```{r, fit models}

m0 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = attitude.data)        # M0: Null (intercept only)
m1 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = attitude.data)     # M1: Complaints
m2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = attitude.data)  # M2: Complaints + Learning
m3 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = attitude.data)  # M3: Expanded
```

**2.3: Exploring the fitted models**

In M1, the complaints coefficient (*b* = 0.76) represents the overall association between complaint handling and ratings: a one-percentage-point increase in favourable responses about complaint handling was associated with a 0.76-point higher overall rating. In M2, after adding learning opportunities, the coefficient dropped to 0.64. It now represents the association between complaint handling and ratings for departments with the same level of learning opportunities. The decrease suggests that part of the M1 association was shared with learning, since departments that handle complaints well also tend to offer more learning opportunities. Adding performance-based raises in M3 left the complaints coefficient essentially unchanged (*b* = 0.65), and the raises coefficient itself was close to zero. This suggests that raises add little beyond complaints and learning.

```{r, nested F tests}
# Comparing all models
nested.tests <- anova(m0, m1, m2, m3) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |>
  rename(
    `Residual df` = Res.Df,
    `Nested df`   = Df,
    `Nested F`    = F,
    `Nested p`    = `Pr(>F)`
  )

nested.tests
```

```{r, model performance}
# model-level statistics for each model
model.performance <- bind_rows(
  glance(m0) |> mutate(Model = "M0: Null"),
  glance(m1) |> mutate(Model = "M1: Complaints"),
  glance(m2) |> mutate(Model = "M2: Complaints + Learning"),
  glance(m3) |> mutate(Model = "M3: Expanded")
) |>
  mutate(RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(residuals(m0)^2)),
    sqrt(mean(residuals(m1)^2)),
    sqrt(mean(residuals(m2)^2)),
    sqrt(mean(residuals(m3)^2))
  )) |>
  select(Model, r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE)

model.performance
```

```{r, delta r squared}
# Change in R-squared relative to the preceding model
model.performance <- model.performance |>
  mutate(delta.r.squared = r.squared - lag(r.squared))

model.performance
```

```{r, model comparison table}
model.comparison <- cbind(model.performance, nested.tests)

model.comparison |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Comparison of Nested Regression Models") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Overall Model Performance",
              columns = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE, `Residual df`)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Incremental Improvement in Fit",
              columns = c(delta.r.squared, `Nested df`, `Nested F`, `Nested p`)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = -c(Model, `Residual df`, `Nested df`), decimals = 3)
```

**3.5: Interpret the comparisons**

M2 and M3 explained the most variation in overall ratings, but almost all of it came from complaint handling. M1 alone explained about 68% of the variation, a large and significant improvement over the null model. Adding learning opportunities explained only about 3% more, and this improvement was not statistically significant. Adding performance-based raises explained virtually nothing further. Adjusted R² rose slightly from M1 to M2 but fell in M3, indicating that raises did not justify the added complexity. Likewise, RMSE dropped substantially from the null model to M1, but the further reductions in M2 and M3 were too small to be meaningful. Overall, complaint handling is the main predictor of workplace ratings, with learning and raises adding little beyond it.

```{r, diagnostics}
#| fig-height: 10
check_model(m2)
check_collinearity(m2)
```

**4.2: Diagnostic Findings**

Diagnostic plots for M2 suggested that most regression assumptions were reasonably satisfied. The residuals showed no systematic curvature, supporting a linear relationship, and they were approximately normally distributed. No department had undue influence on the fitted model; the most influential observation was the lowest-rated department noted earlier, but its influence was well below conventional thresholds. Multicollinearity was low, so although complaint handling and learning opportunities are correlated, their separate contributions can still be estimated. The main concern was heteroscedasticity: residual variability was larger for departments with lower predicted ratings, so the model’s predictions are less precise for poorly rated departments. This could make the standard errors, and therefore the p-values and confidence intervals, somewhat inaccurate. However, the coefficient estimates themselves remain unbiased, and with only 30 departments this pattern may partly reflect a few low-rated departments. Overall, the diagnostics do not substantially undermine confidence in the model, but inferences about learning opportunities, whose effect was already uncertain, should be interpreted cautiously.

**5.1: Selecting a model**

I selected M2 (complaints and learning) as the preferred model. M3 can be ruled out: adding performance-based raises explained essentially no additional variation, was not statistically significant, and lowered adjusted R², so it added complexity without improving fit. The choice between M1 and M2 is less clear. Adding learning did not significantly improve fit, and the gains in R² and RMSE were small, which favours the simpler M1. However, M2 had the highest adjusted R² of the four models, indicating that the improvement in fit outweighed the cost of the extra predictor. Including learning also makes the model more substantively interpretable, because it estimates the association between complaint handling and ratings while holding learning opportunities constant, rather than letting complaint handling absorb variation shared with learning. The diagnostics supported this choice: multicollinearity between the two predictors was low, and no observations were unduly influential. Given that the evidence for learning is uncertain, its coefficient should be interpreted cautiously, but M2 provides the most informative and still parsimonious account of overall workplace ratings.

```{r, coefficient table}
m2.coefs <- tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE)

m2.coefs |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Coefficients for M2: Predicting Overall Workplace Rating")
```

```{r, coefficient values}
comp <- m2.coefs |> filter(term == "complaints")
learn <- m2.coefs |> filter(term == "learning")
```

Both predictors were positively associated with overall workplace ratings. Holding learning opportunities constant, a one-percentage-point increase in favourable responses about complaint handling was associated with a `{r} round(pull(comp, estimate), 2)`-point increase in a department's overall rating (95% CI \[`{r} round(pull(comp, conf.low), 2)`, `{r} round(pull(comp, conf.high), 2)`\]). This interval lies entirely above zero, so complaint handling has a clearly positive association with ratings. Holding complaint handling constant, a one-percentage-point increase in favourable responses about learning opportunities was associated with a `{r} round(pull(learn, estimate), 2)`-point increase in overall rating (95% CI \[`{r} round(pull(learn, conf.low), 2)`, `{r} round(pull(learn, conf.high), 2)`\]). However, this interval includes zero, so the data are consistent with learning having a small positive association, no association, or even a slight negative one. Its unique contribution beyond complaint handling therefore remains uncertain.

```{r, m2 performance}
m2.perf <- model.performance |> filter(Model == "M2: Complaints + Learning")
```

The selected model explained `{r} round(pull(m2.perf, r.squared) * 100, 1)`% of the variation in overall workplace ratings across departments (adjusted R² = `{r} round(pull(m2.perf, adj.r.squared), 2)`). This means complaint handling and learning opportunities together account for most of the differences in how departments rate their workplace. Adjusted R² is only slightly lower than R², indicating that the fit is not inflated by unnecessary predictors. The RMSE of `{r} round(pull(m2.perf, RMSE), 2)` means the model's predicted ratings typically differ from departments' actual ratings by about this many points. Given that ratings ranged from 40 to 85, this is a moderate level of error: the model captures the main pattern well, but it cannot predict any single department's rating precisely.

**Part 6- Findings and Limitations**

These results suggest that complaint handling is by far the most important of the three predictors of overall workplace ratings. It accounted for most of the explained variation and remained a strong predictor regardless of which other variables were included. Learning opportunities appeared to play a smaller supporting role, but their unique contribution was uncertain once complaint handling was taken into account. Performance-based raises added nothing beyond the other two predictors, likely because they overlap with what complaints and learning already capture. Together, this suggests that how responsive management is to employees matters more for overall impressions of a workplace than opportunities for growth or reward.

Several limitations should be considered. With only 30 departments, the estimates are imprecise, and the study may have lacked the power to detect smaller effects such as that of learning. Because the data are department-level averages, the results describe differences between departments and may not apply to individual employees. The data are also cross-sectional and observational, so the associations cannot be interpreted as causal; for example, employees who already rate their workplace highly may also view its complaint handling more favourably. Finally, the unequal residual variance identified in the diagnostics means the standard errors and confidence intervals may be somewhat inaccurate, particularly for lower-rated departments.
